p: On March fifteenth Ana filed. She asked the court to test the scrapings from under Travis Hensley's nails, untouched for nineteen years, and for a new trial.

Her card for new evidence has four lines. The jury never heard it. The defense couldn't have known it, with reasonable care. It's about what happened, not only about whether somebody's believable. It would probably bring an acquittal.
At his thirtieth birthday Teo was angry about the boy in the newspaper. Then he said they never found the flashlight. Nobody had ever said there was one.
Dani wrote his words down with the date, and she didn't call him.
The two of them did agree on one thing: Lupe hears about her grandfather from them, before she turns seven.
Luis Ruiz. Dani's driving up to Sterling to see him for the first time since last July.
Ana Brennan. Dani's teacher Tuesday and Thursday nights, and every other Saturday.
Ronnie Galvan. The bartender from that night. He still runs the taqueria.
Joel Harlan. Dani's supervisor, still asking about law school.

Thursday, April 15. Ana had cleared the whole desk for once. No freezer bag, no blue copy, no motion. Two pages from Phil's trial binder lay side by side under the lamp, and Dicta lay under the desk with her chin on Ana's shoe.

Saturday the week before, at six in the morning, Dani had sent an email to an address at Sterling Correctional Facility asking for a contact visit on April 17. Six, because that was the first morning they'd take a request for that date, and the slots went to whoever asked first. The answer came Monday. Approved. Bring your photo ID.

She hadn't been up since July, a hot Saturday, before any of this. They'd played on a board from the desk that day, a cardboard one with a corner gone soft, and talked about the Rockies the whole time, and she'd driven home with the radio loud.
Eight weeks to June. When she told him on Wednesday that she was coming, the line went quiet. Then: Don't wear a jacket. They make you leave it outside.

Thursday afternoon, before she left the office, Joel had stopped at her desk with a file under his arm and asked for the suppression motion by Monday, and then, as if it were the same sentence, whether she'd looked at schools. She had. Two she could drive to, and she'd been reading about part time programs, the kind you did at night. She said nights, because at night she could keep the job. You can keep a job either way, he said. Don't make this office the reason. I've watched it be the reason for people. He set the file down on her keyboard. Tuesday's fine for the motion.

Now, across the desk, Ana didn't look up. You're not his lawyer on Saturday, she said. I'm his lawyer. You're his daughter. Don't interview him. Visit him. And if he says something? Then you heard it. And you drive home and call me.
She picked up the pencil. Tonight, shapes.
April on Federal, and somebody downstairs is washing a load of horse blankets, from the smell. Dicta is offended. Pencil.

You've spent since October taking arguments apart. Tonight you take two apart at once and ask whether they're built the same. A parallel reasoning question gives you an argument and five more, on five other subjects, and asks which one reasons the way the first one does. The subject doesn't matter. Foxes, folders, bridges, bread. What matters is the bones.

So you strip it. Every claim gets a letter and loses its topic. The tracks show a limp; the fox that made them is one of two; only one of the two limps; so it was that one. Bones: X has a trait, X belongs to a small group, only one member of the group has the trait, so X is that member. Write the bones in the margin before you read a single choice. If you can't write them, you haven't read the argument yet.

Then start from the conclusion, because that's where the quick eliminations are. Look at what kind of claim it is. A must, a probably, a should, a some, a never. If the original concludes that something should be done, an answer that concludes something will happen is gone, however close the rest looks. If the original says probably, an answer that says certainly is gone. Match the conclusion's type and its strength first, then check the premises.

Here's a drill that keeps the three things you match apart. One argument: every juror on the panel took the oath, Ruiz is on the panel, so Ruiz took the oath. Bones: all A are B, this one is A, so it's B. Now change one thing at a time. Change only the topic: every boat in the harbor carries flares, the Nell is in the harbor, so the Nell carries flares. Still parallel. Change the counting word: most jurors took the oath, Ruiz is a juror, so Ruiz took it. Not parallel anymore. Most only gets you probably, so a conclusion that Ruiz did take it is a flaw. Change the force: every juror took the oath, Ruiz is a juror, so Ruiz should take it. Should isn't did. Do that with five arguments of your own on a Sunday afternoon until a new topic stops fooling you and a changed word starts to shout.

Order doesn't matter. An argument can put its conclusion first and its rule last and still be the same argument. Two answers will often use the same pieces as the original and arrange them so they run backward, or drop one piece, or soften an all to a most. Those are the ones that feel right and aren't.

One more thing, and it's the thing people forget. Same shape says nothing about true. A good shape can carry false premises all day, and a bad shape can land on a true conclusion by luck. This question doesn't ask you to judge anything. It asks you to match.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which argument is most similar in its reasoning to the one above, or which one exhibits a pattern of reasoning most similar to it. Write the bones first, match the conclusion's type and strength, and only then check the premises.

The cousin of that question tells you the original argument is flawed and asks which answer is flawed the same way. Parallel flaw. Here you name the mistake before you look for its twin. Treats a requirement as a guarantee. Takes a trait lots of people have as proof it's one person. Says nobody found it, so it isn't there, when nobody looked.

Name it in plain words, then go through the choices asking one thing: does this one make that mistake? Not a mistake. That one. An argument with a different flaw is wrong, and so is an argument with no flaw at all. That second trap gets people every time. A choice that reasons correctly can look almost exactly like the original, with one extra word, an only or a probably, that quietly fixes it. Fixed isn't parallel.
If two choices both seem to make the mistake, go back to the bones and compare the shape of the claims too. The right answer usually matches both the flaw and the structure around it.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which argument's flawed reasoning is most similar to the reasoning above, or which exhibits a flaw most like the original's. Name the flaw in plain words before you read the choices.

A method question doesn't ask what someone concluded. It asks how they got there, or how they answered somebody else. The right answer describes the move in general words. Offers a counterexample. Points to a similar case. Questions the source. Rules out the other possibility. Turns to a different issue.

Read every word of the description against the argument. These answers fail on one word. If the choice says the speaker attacks the other person's character, and the speaker only questions a fact, it's wrong. If it says two cases, and there's one, it's wrong. A description has to be true of the argument all the way through.

People are slipperier than arguments, by the way. When somebody doesn't want to answer you, they rarely refuse. They answer a different question, one that sounds near enough, often one about you. Notice when the subject changes, and say what it changed to.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask how the argument proceeds, which describes the technique of reasoning, or how one speaker responds to another. Test each word of a choice against what the speaker actually did.

Once per Reading Comprehension section, usually, you get two shorter passages on one subject instead of one long one. Read the first the ordinary way: main point, attitude, the job each paragraph does. Then read the second one and work out what it has to do with the first. Sometimes the second author is arguing with the first. Plenty of times they've never met. Two scientists wrote about the same birds, years apart, and neither one cites the other. Then there's no reply to find. You're looking for where they line up, where they split, and what one talks about that the other never mentions.

The relationships come in a few kinds. They agree, and one adds something. They agree on the facts and fight about what they mean. One takes the other's idea somewhere new, or both try the same idea on different cases. They disagree outright, which is rarer than people expect. Most pairs share a good deal and part on one point. Find the point. And don't invent a reply where nobody replied.

Here's how to keep from inventing one. Before you name a relationship, ask a single question. Does either passage mention the other's claim, its evidence or its author? If neither does, you've got two people looking at one thing, and the relationship is about overlap. Both describe the same finding and draw different lessons from it. One explains a cause and the other only reports the effect. One looks at a narrow case and the other at the whole. Say a geologist writes about why a lake in the Andes is shrinking, and some years later an anthropologist writes about a village on its shore moving its fields uphill. Neither cites the other. A good answer says both treat the lake's shrinking as real, and only the first explains it. A bad one says the second author challenges the first, or builds on the first. Nobody built anything. They stood on the same shore.

The questions ask about both passages, or one, or how they relate. When a question asks what both authors would accept, it's the yes and yes test from March. Each author has to be committed to it, from what's on the page.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which statement both authors would most likely agree with, how the two passages relate, or how one author would likely respond to a claim in the other. Don't assume either author has read the other. Decide the relationship in a sentence before you start the questions.

The last one is the parallel question in Reading Comprehension clothes. A passage describes a situation, and the question asks which of five others is most like it. Strip it the same way. Who did what, to whom, for what reason, with what result. Then find the choice with the same relationships, whatever the subject.

The trap is a choice that shares the subject and not the relationship. If the passage is about a scientist who reports a careful finding and somebody else stretches it, the wrong answer is the other scientist story. The right one might be about a bakery.

Let's work one all the way. A passage says a climbing vine finds the tallest tree near it by sensing the shade the tree throws, not the tree itself. The question asks which is most analogous to the vine's method. Name the relationship first: it finds a thing by the effect the thing has on what's around it. Now the choices. A gardener who trains vines up tall trees shares the subject and none of the relationship. A sailor who finds an island by the clouds that pile up over land, before the land is in sight, is the analogy. Different world, same move.

The common error is taking the choice with the most matching nouns. Next comes matching half the relationship. Picture a sailor who just looks and sees the island. He found it, sure. Not by its effect, though, so he's out. Sometimes the stem asks about a person, not a process. Which is most similar to the critic's reasoning? To the town's response? Same work. What did they do, and why? Put it in words that would fit a bakery or a war. Then find the choice those words fit.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which situation is most analogous to the one described, or which is most similar to the relationship between two things in the passage. Name the relationship in plain words, then ignore every choice's topic.

Parallel questions get fast once you stop reading them as stories. Every argument has three things you can match: its counting words, its structure, and the force of its conclusion. A choice has to match all three. The topic is the one thing it never has to match, and the test spends most of its wrong answers on people who match the topic.

Start with the counting words, because they're on a ladder. At the top: all, every, each, none, never, always. Below that, most, which means more than half. Below that, some and at least one, which mean one or more and promise nothing past it. Many and several sit with some on this test. Many gets you at least some, several gets you more than one, and neither one reaches most. If the original climbs to most, the match has to climb to most. A choice that says all where the original said most hasn't kept the shape. It's made a stronger argument with different bones.

Then the force of the conclusion, which is its own ladder. Must, certainly, has to: the top rung. Probably, likely, is reason to believe: the middle. Could, may, might: the bottom. And off to the side, two rungs on their own ladders. Should is a recommendation, not a prediction. Caused is a claim about why, not about what. A conclusion that says the plan should go ahead can't be matched by one that says it will work. A conclusion that says the rain caused the delays can't be matched by one that says the rain and the delays came together.

Then the structure, the bones you already know. All A are B, this is A, so it's B. If A then B, not B, so not A. Either A or B, not A, so B. Most A are B and most A are C, so some B are C. Write it short and in plain parts. When the original has two premises and a conclusion, a match with three premises might still be fine, if the third is background. A match with one premise missing isn't.

Here's the order I'd work them in. Conclusion first: its type and its rung. That kills two or three choices in ten seconds, and you haven't read their premises yet. Then the counting words in the premises. Then the structure, on whatever's left. If two choices survive all three, read them both once more for a word that runs the arrow backward. There usually is one.

Work one with me. The argument goes like this. Most of the cyclists in the club ride carbon frames, and most of the cyclists in the club ride on clip in pedals. So at least one cyclist in the club rides a carbon frame on clip in pedals. Bones: most and most of the same group, so some overlap. Conclusion: the bottom rung of the counting ladder, at least one, and stated as certain, which it can be, because two majorities of one group have to touch. Valid.

Now the choices, the way they'd come. Some of the guests ordered fish and some ordered soup, so at least one guest ordered both. That's dropped a rung: two somes don't have to touch. Out. Most of the guests ordered fish and most of those who ordered fish also ordered soup, so most guests ordered soup. The second most counts a different room, the fish eaters, and the conclusion climbed to most. Out. Most of the guests ordered fish, so most guests probably didn't order soup. Different structure, and a probably. Out. A choice about cyclists who ride carbon frames and clip ins and win races: same topic, a third claim the original never made. Out. And then: more than half the tenants in the building have a dog, and more than half the tenants have a car, so some tenant has both a dog and a car. Most and most of one group, some overlap, stated as certain. That's the match, and it's about dogs.

Parallel flaw works the same way with one more step: the match has to make the original's mistake, at the original's strength. If the original slides from most to all, the match slides from most to all, not from some to most. If the original treats a requirement as a guarantee, the match does too, and a choice that treats a guarantee as a requirement has made the other mistake. Same family, different flaw, and it's wrong.

Drill this one away from the test. Write one argument on a card. Then write four versions of it. In one change only the topic. In one change only a counting word. In one change only the force of the conclusion. In one turn an arrow around. Hand the stack to somebody and have them shuffle it. Pick out the parallel one. When you can do it without reading the topics, you're ready.

How the exam asks it. On parallel and parallel flaw questions, check each choice's conclusion first for type and strength, then its counting words, then its structure. A choice that shares the topic but changes any one of the three is a trap.

A paired set, the questions only, so you can hear how the three lists work. Passage A is an engineer writing about why old stone bridges in one valley have outlasted the steel ones built a century later: the stone works only in compression, and nothing in it rusts. Passage B is a local historian writing about the same valley's bridges as gathering places, where markets were held and news was passed, and about how the steel bridges built later, for trucks, had no room for any of that. Neither mentions the other.

First, the lists. Overlap: both say the valley has old stone bridges and later steel ones. Split: nothing, really. Neither says a word against the other. Only in A: why stone lasts. Only in B: what the bridges were used for, and what was lost.

Now the questions. How do the passages relate? Both discuss the valley's stone and steel bridges, A in terms of how they're built and B in terms of how people used them. A choice that says B disputes A's account of the bridges' strength invents a fight. Which would both authors accept? That the valley's stone bridges came before its steel ones. Both say so. A choice that says the stone bridges are better ought to make you check: A thinks they last longer, B thinks they served people better, and better isn't the same claim in both mouths. What does A discuss that B doesn't? How stone carries a load. What would the author of B most likely say about A's point that stone lasts longer? Nothing in B tells you its author would deny it. They might take it as one more reason the old bridges matter, but the safe answer stays small.
That last move, keeping the answer small, is the whole skill. When the passages never met, every connection you draw between them has to be built from lines that are actually on the page.

How the exam asks it. For an independent pair, the relationship answer usually says both discuss one subject from different angles. Be suspicious of any choice that has one passage dispute, support or respond to the other.
Ana had written the State's case on an index card the way she wrote everything worth keeping, in capitals, in pencil, with no adjectives anywhere.

Ana's card, the State's bones. THE STATE, BONES ONLY. 1. THE MAN AT THE CURB WORE A RED JACKET. 2. HE WAS A MAN TRAVIS FOUGHT IN THE BAR. (THE GUY FROM THE BAR.). 3. OF THE MEN IN THAT FIGHT, ONLY LUIS WORE ONE. SO: THE MAN AT THE CURB WAS LUIS.

Look at it like it's a stranger's, she said. If all three lines are true, the last one has to be. That's a good shape. It's what makes it dangerous. She laid four more cards in a row under it, every one about Mrs. Haugen's hens and the foxes up in the north woods. One of these has the same bones. Ignore the foxes.
A. Tracks by the coop show a limp. The only fox in the county that limps is the old one from the north woods. So he got the hens.
B. The old one of the two north woods foxes limps, and the young one's a lot quicker. Whatever got the hens was one of them. So it was the old one.
C. Whatever got the hens was one of the two north woods foxes. Of those two, only the old one limps. The tracks limp. So it was him.
D. The old fox out of the north woods limps, and the tracks by the coop show a limp too. So the old fox got the hens last night.

Dani slides one card out of the row. The hens went to one of two foxes, only the old one limps, the tracks limp, so it was him. Same bones, Ana says. Out of order, which is allowed. A trait, a small group, one member with the trait. Every line true, the last one has to be. She taps line two on her own card, the guy from the bar. You don't go after the shape, then. You go after a line.

That's the one. Pencil down. Parallel reasoning. Strip the State's card and you get a man with a trait, a small group he belongs to, and only one person in that group with the trait, so he's that person. The fox card has all four, shuffled. Shuffling is allowed. Topic doesn't count. Structure does.
Decision two. The one in the room.
Ana turned the card over. On the back, smaller: MAN AT THE CURB WORE RED. LUIS WORE RED. SO LUIS WAS THE MAN AT THE CURB.

That's the one the jury heard, she said. Whatever the closing said out loud, that's what twelve people carried into the room. It's broken. You know how. Now find me its twin. Same mistake, nothing added and nothing fixed.
A. "The woman who took the umbrella wore a green raincoat. Inez had one on that day. So Inez took the umbrella."
B. "Inez had a green raincoat on that day. So did the woman who took the umbrella. So Inez could be the one who took it."
C. "Nobody saw any woman but Inez near the umbrella rack that whole day. So Inez is the one who took the umbrella from it."
D. "Only one woman in the lobby wore a green raincoat, and the woman who took the umbrella wore one. Inez did. So Inez took it."
Twins, Ana says. A thing plenty of people have, treated like a thing one person has. Green raincoat, red jacket. Nobody counted either. She writes COUNT on the back of the card and underlines it.

Right. Now say why. Parallel flaw. A trait the culprit had, which the suspect also has, treated as proof the suspect is the culprit. Lots of women own green raincoats, and lots of men wore red that night. Same mistake, same size.
Then the two pages under the lamp. The prosecution's closing on the left, the one Dani had read in October with the binder's rubber band breaking in her hand. On the right, a page she'd never seen.

Trial transcript, Monday, June 9, 2008, the prosecution's closing argument. Consuelo Baca never saw a face. She told you that herself, and you can trust a witness who tells you what she didn't see. What she saw was a man in a red jacket strike Travis Hensley at a quarter past eleven and run. So who wore a red jacket that night? The defendant did. His own daughter told you he wore it to work that day. Ronnie Galvan told you the defendant and Travis fought inside the bar less than an hour before. The lab told you Travis Hensley's blood was on the cuff. And the next morning, before any officer knocked, that jacket was in the washer, in a house where he never did the laundry. The defendant told police he never touched anyone. The blood on his cuff says he did. People don't wash what they aren't worried about. Put it together, and the man in the red jacket was Luis Ruiz.

Trial transcript, Monday, June 9, 2008, the defense closing argument. Mrs. Baca told you the truth. She saw a man in a red jacket, and she never saw his face. So ask yourselves how many red jackets were in that bar. Luis Ruiz works at Platte Valley Refining, and so does every man on his crew, and every one of them wears that jacket. His daughter told you so. Mr. Galvan says there was a scuffle inside, and men bleed in scuffles. Blood on a cuff tells you there was a bar. It doesn't tell you there was a parking lot. A work jacket went in the washer on a Sunday, which is where work jackets go. The State had to show you it was this man, in this jacket, at that curb. It showed you a jacket.

Ana slid Phil's page over next to the other one so the edges lined up. Phil's, she said. Read them as a pair, the way you'd read two witnesses to the same thing. How does the second one line up against the first?
A. It disputes the State's facts one by one and says its witnesses were wrong about them.
B. It grants the State's main facts and says they fit other men, or innocent reasons.
C. It uses Consuelo's own words to argue that the man at the curb couldn't have been Luis.
D. It names another man from the refinery crew and argues he's the one who struck Travis.

Phil's page gives the State its facts, Dani says, and then shows they fit other men, or a reason nobody has to hide. Every one, Ana says. The jacket, yes, twenty jackets. The blood, yes, from a bar. The washer, yes, it's a work jacket. He took their pieces one at a time and showed the jury each one fit more than one picture. She runs the pencil down Phil's page. Not bad. Not enough.

Good. That's how you read it. Comparative passages. Phil grants the jacket, the blood and the washer and gives each another explanation. He doesn't deny the State's facts. He disputes what they show. That's the relationship.
Ana put her finger on the prosecution's first line. Consuelo Baca never saw a face.
She gave him a color. He gave the jury a man. That's what he did with her, start to finish. Another row of cards, a white van in each. Find me that somewhere else. Not a courtroom.
A. The neighbor reports the van and names the driver, then later admits she only guessed at who was behind the wheel.
B. The neighbor got a clear look at the driver's face as well as the van, and the landlord, checking her story, finds the tenant's cousin.
C. The neighbor reports the van but never saw the driver. The landlord finds out the tenant's cousin drives one and bills him.
D. The neighbor saw nothing at all that night. The landlord quotes her as having seen the van parked at the empty house.

Dani picks the neighbor who never saw a driver, and the landlord who finds out the tenant's cousin drives a white van and bills him anyway. That's her, Ana says. She said exactly what she saw and nothing more. The landlord did the rest and used her name to do it. Dani thinks of the confession booth, every Saturday for a year.

That's the one. Pencil down. Analogy. In the closing, a witness's careful, limited account, a color and no face, is joined to other facts and used for an identification she never made. The neighbor and the landlord have the same relationship.
Dani read the two pages again, the left and then the right. Two lawyers, two hours apart on the same Monday, going opposite ways.
Now what they agree on without saying it, Ana said. Both of them stood up and took something for granted. What?
A. That the man at the curb came out of that bar, so the only question was which of its men.
B. That the man Consuelo saw at the curb was wearing a ball cap as well as the red jacket.
C. That Luis never laid a hand on Travis Hensley at any point that night, inside the bar or out.
D. That the jacket Consuelo saw was a Platte Valley work jacket, the same as the one Luis wore.

They both take it for granted, Dani says, that the man at the curb came out of that bar. That bar, Ana says. The prosecutor goes straight from the curb to the fight inside. Phil says how many jackets were in that bar. Neither one ever looks outside it. And neither of them says cap. No, Ana says. Phil argued their case with better manners.

Right. Now say why. Comparative passages. The prosecutor goes from the curb straight to the fight inside, and Phil counts the jackets in that bar. Both of them are treating the attacker as one of the customers. Neither one ever says it out loud.

Ana tapped the dispatch log in its sleeve. So Phil had this, she said. Tabbed. Highlighted, half of it. And he stood up in front of that jury and argued the face, and the jackets, and the washer, and he never said cap. She looked at his page a while. What's that like? She dealt another row.
A. The student shows the teacher's own email admitting a scoring error, and the grade gets changed that afternoon.
B. The student invents an email from the teacher admitting an error, and argues from the email.
C. The student has no proof of any error at all, and argues that the test ran long and was unfair.
D. The student has the teacher's email admitting a scoring error, and argues only that the test ran long.

Dani picks the student with the teacher's email in hand, who argues about the clock instead. That's him, Ana says. Then, quieter, to the page and not to Dani: I'd know it anywhere. She doesn't say why. Dani thinks of a brief with nine issues, and the jacket ninth, and doesn't say anything either.

Good. That's how you read it. Analogy. The student holds the decisive document and argues weaker points instead. Phil had the dispatch log with the cap in it and argued the face, the jackets and the washer. Same relationship.

Saturday, April 17. She left at a quarter to six in the dark, up I-76 with the heater on and the radio off, and somewhere past Hudson the sky went gray and then pink over the fields. Feedlots. A grain elevator with a town's name painted on it. Long stretches with nothing on either side but wind.
At ten to eight she was parked in the visitors' lot with the engine off, looking at two lines of fence and a low tan building, and she had an hour and forty minutes.
Ana had sent her a photo the night before, without a word. The last paragraph of Gene's 2007 summary, typed on a machine with a sticky e.
Detective G. Vigil, case summary, October 29, 2007, last paragraph. Witnesses at the scene did not report any other male in a confrontation with the victim. No other suspect was developed.

She knew what sat under that paragraph, because she'd read it all. Patrons' names not obtained. The bar empty before the first car came. A refinery crew list Gene got from the shift supervisor and never called. She wrote it out on the inside cover of her prep book the way Ana would: nobody reported another man; nobody asked; so there wasn't one. Then she went looking for its twin, in a set at the back of the book that was all one hotel and the noise on its fourth floor.
A. Every guest on that floor was asked about noise, and none reported any, so there probably isn't much.
B. No guests reported noise up there, so there's none. The hotel only asked guests on the first three floors.
C. The manager says there's no noise problem up there, and the manager is never wrong, so there isn't one.
D. All the guests up there complained about noise, so every floor in the hotel must have a noise problem.

The hotel that never asked the fourth floor. Same hole. You can't report what nobody asks you about. She circles it, and then she circles did not report in Gene's paragraph, on her phone, with her thumb, which does nothing at all.

That's the one. Pencil down. Parallel flaw. No report, from people who were never asked, taken as proof there's nothing to report. The hotel never asked the fourth floor, and nobody asked the crew. Same mistake.

Her phone went in the glove box with the prep book and the envelope. Her jacket stayed on the seat. Inside, at the desk, she showed her license and the one debit card they let you bring for the machines, and a woman in a fleece vest handed her a laminated card to read while she waited.

Card at the visiting desk. Bring one photo ID and one debit or credit card. No phones, watches, books or papers past this desk. Coats, jackets, hats and hoods stay outside. Except for vending machine items, nothing passes between visitor and resident. A brief hug at the start and end of the visit. You may hold hands on top of the table. Games go back to the desk thirty minutes before visiting ends.

It was cold in there, like he'd said, and bright. Round tables bolted down, the machines on one wall, a TV up in a corner with the sound off showing a golf tournament nobody was watching. He came through the far door in the green they all wore. Older than his voice. Grayer, thinner through the shoulders. Then he saw her and grinned and walked too fast, and the officer said something, and he slowed down about one step's worth.
They got the short hug the card allowed. Into her hair he said, You got tall. She'd been this tall since she was fourteen.

Two coffees from the machine, on her debit card. His stayed on his side of the table. Rules. The woman at the desk had a cardboard chess set in a box with a rubber band on it, and Dani signed for it on a clipboard with a pen on a string. No notes. He set up his side and she set up hers, and when he got to the bishop he put it on her knight's square without looking up. She let him.
Lupe's crown for a while. The glitter glue. How Lupe wore it herself in the end. Your brother? Thirty, she said. I know how old he is.
She'd driven two hours to ask it to his face. Pa. Ronnie says you swung first.

He looked at the board a long time. On the phone that one always came back fast, before she finished asking. Not today. I hit him first. He didn't say anything else for a while. Then, to the bishop: He put his hands on a kid. What kid? Some kid. Nobody. He picked up his coffee and put it down without drinking any. You look tired, mija. Eight weeks out from your test and you drive up here in the dark. You eating? Brennan has you up till midnight, I bet. You should be home with your book.
What did Pa just do with her question?
A. "I asked who the kid was, Pa, and you're asking if I'm eating."
B. "You're trying to make me feel bad for driving all the way up here today, Pa."
C. "You're saying the kid doesn't matter because nothing bad ever happened to him."
D. "You're saying Ronnie got it wrong and you never swung at that man first."
He looks at her a long moment, and then he almost smiles. Eat something on the way home, he says, which is the same move again, and they both hear it.
Right. Now say why. Method of reasoning. She asked about the kid, and he turned to her test, her sleep and her eating. He didn't refuse. He changed the subject to what she needs. That's the move.

After, Ronnie threw me out, and I went home. By myself. He said the going home part to the board, in the same words he'd given Gene in 2007 and her on a hundred Wednesdays since. A man who just got thrown out of a bar for fighting goes home, mija. He doesn't go back out looking for more. I got thrown out. So I went home.

At the next table a little boy in light up shoes was trying to climb into his father's lap, and his mother kept telling him not yet, not yet, baby, and the shoes kept flashing red against the table leg. Dani watched them for a second. Then she answered her father the way he'd taught her to answer a move on the garage sale board, with a move of her own.
Which line about Benny has the same shape as Pa's argument about going home?
A. "Benny, then. He resigned, so he must have lost his queen to somebody right before it."
B. "Benny, then. A player who just lost his queen resigns. Benny just lost his queen. So Benny resigned."
C. "Benny, then. Most players who lose their queen resign, so Benny probably did when he lost his."
D. "Benny, then. Nobody ever saw Benny keep playing, so I guess Benny quit the game."

He laughs, the real laugh, and the woman at the desk looks up from her clipboard. Benny never resigns, he says. Benny plays every game out to the last pawn and then wants to shake on it. When he's finished he asks if that makes it a bad argument, and she says no, it makes it a shape, and a shape can't tell you if something is true. He asks what does, then. Somebody who checks, she says. Like Brennan, he says. Like me. He laughs again, shorter, and looks at the bishop.

Good. That's how you read it. Parallel reasoning. He takes a rule about anybody in a situation and applies it to himself: thrown out men go home, he got thrown out, so he went home. Benny's argument is built the same way. Matching the shape doesn't tell you anything about whether it's true. Benny, who has never resigned a game in his life, is how a rule like that fails.

It was right there. He'd told Gene in 2007 he never touched anybody. He'd told her the same thing on the phone in January, fast, before she'd even finished asking. Now he'd told her, across a cardboard board, that it wasn't true. So the rest of it was a lie too. Going home was a lie. The whole thing. That step was easy. Too easy. She'd missed the bottom stair at home that way a hundred times, in the dark, going down for the laundry.
He was watching her face. He'd been reading it since she was eight. Go on, he said. Say it. You left the house before six for this.
A. "I won't say it, Pa. It'd be like saying the cook never burns anything, so he couldn't have burned this toast."
B. "You lied to Gene about the punch, Pa. So you lied about going home too. Where'd you really go?"
C. "I won't say it. It'd be like the cook burning the toast once, so he'll probably burn the eggs too."
D. "I won't say it, Pa. It'd be like burning one piece of toast and deciding every piece on the plate's burned."

He doesn't answer right away. At the next table the boy has made it into his father's lap at last, and the mother is reading the vending machine prices out loud to no one in particular. You're not going to say it, her father says. She says no. He says okay. It's what he used to say at the kitchen table when she took a move back and he let her. His hand goes around his paper cup on his side of the table and stays there.

That's the one. Pencil down. Parallel flaw. Her thought would jump from one proven lie to everything he's said, the same jump as from one burned slice of toast to the whole plate. One false claim doesn't show the others are false.
At three the woman at the desk called it. Games back, folks. Thirty minutes.
That's been sitting there since January, her father said, about the bishop.
It was still on her knight's old square. Two of her pawns could take it. She went for the one next to her king, the one Lupe had poked at in January, and stopped with her hand over it.

She'd never once looked at the whole board on the basement step. She looked now. If that pawn took, the file in front of her king opened up, and his queen had been sitting at the far end of it for weeks. Teo had said it in January, in her kitchen, zipping Lupe's coat with grease to his elbows: he gives you something easy to take, so you're busy taking it.
She took with the other pawn.

He sat back. Huh. Then, softer: Your brother always took with the other one. The one by the king. Every time. Ten years old. She said she knew. Teo told her, January, at her table. Her father looked at her, then at the board, a long time. He remembered that, he said.

The woman came around for the box. Dani said the position over once in her head, for the board at home, and the pieces went back in the cardboard with the rubber band. Then he wanted Brennan's argument. Short, he said. Like I'm Rudy.
She put it in refinery terms. He'd done fourteen years at one.
Which spill story most closely parallels Brennan's argument?
A. "Say the foreman blames you for a spill. If your valve was open, you caused it. Your valve was open. So you did."
B. "Say a foreman pins a spill on you because your valve was the only one open. Three were. So it was one of the others."
C. "A foreman blames you for a spill because yours was the only valve open. Three were open. So he hasn't shown it was you."
D. "Say the foreman blames you for a spill, since yours was the only open valve. Three were open. So it wasn't you."

So she's not saying I didn't do it. She's saying they never showed that you did. He nods, slowly, and turns his cup. That's a smaller thing. It's the whole thing, Pa. Smart woman, he says. Rudy would get that. Rudy would want it on a card.

Right. Now say why. Parallel reasoning. My argument: the identification rested on Luis being the only man in red; he wasn't; so the State didn't prove it was him. The valve version has the same parts and the same modest ending, that the reason fails, not that the opposite is true.

By three twenty there was nothing on the table but their two paper cups. Pa. The kid, she said, and he said, Nobody, mija, quietly. Let it be nobody. After that he told her to tell Brennan yes on the swab, that she'd asked in her letter. And tell her she wasn't wrong. He'd had that ready. Probably since March.

She'd had hers ready since December, since the night at the kitchen table with the envelope. Pa, I'm not sure you didn't. She put her hand over his. The card said you could. Pa, I'm not, she said. He waited. Somebody's debit card beeped at the machine by the wall and a bag of chips dropped. The kid in the light up shoes was asleep on his dad now with one shoe still going. I'm not going to make it back up here before the test, she said, and he said good, study.
His hand turned over under hers and stayed there.
The hug at the end was supposed to be short, and the officer by the door gave them an extra second anyway and looked at his clipboard.

Outside the wind had come up hard enough to rock the car on its springs. She got her phone out of the glove box and called Ana before she'd even put her jacket back on. Ana picked up on the first ring and said well. Dani told her. He swung first, because some man had his hands on a kid. Ana didn't say anything. Then she asked what kid, and Dani said he says nobody.

Ana was quiet long enough for a truck to go by on Federal behind her. When Ana came back she was doing Meredith, flatter and faster, the way she always did it. All right. He admits he hit Travis Hensley first. So he's a man who'd hit Travis Hensley. A man who'd hit him once in a bar is capable of the rest of it in a parking lot. What's wrong with that?
A. "He only swung because Travis grabbed a kid, Ana. Anybody would've done the same."
B. "She can't use it. He's only said it to me at a table, never once in court."
C. "A punch in a bar isn't the same thing as hitting a man with something at a curb."
D. "Capable isn't did. Half that bar was capable. She'd still need him at the curb."

That's the sentence, Ana says, and tells her to write it down before she starts the car, on anything she's got. Dani finds a napkin in the glove box from a burrito place in Fort Morgan and writes it on her knee in capitals. Dani, Ana says. Drive slow.

Good. That's how you read it. Flaw. The argument goes from could have to did. Plenty of people are capable of plenty of things, so capable doesn't pick out this man. Meredith would still have to put him at the curb.
She sat in the car with the engine off and her phone in her lap, and she didn't start it.
Some neighbor kid, mija. That was March, on the phone. Some kid. Nobody. That was at the table, with his coffee in his hand. Nobody, mija. Let it be nobody. That was twenty minutes ago.

Three times he'd put the kid down the way Ana put down a conclusion, at the end, where everything else was supposed to hold it up. Except nothing held it up. A man doesn't swing first for nobody. Not him. Not the man who used to carry her report cards around in his wallet and show them to the whole bar.

And the bishop. He'd taken her knight with it in January and left it sitting there, something easy to take. Today, with the whole board in front of her, she'd seen what the easy take would open, and she hadn't made it. And he'd put the punch down on the table the same way, and she'd taken it, and kept on taking it, and quit looking at the rest of the board. She'd seen it on the board. She hadn't seen it at the table.

She called the taqueria. Whoever picked up yelled for Ronnie without covering the phone. It went down on the counter. A fryer, a radio in back, somebody arguing about a delivery. Then Ronnie, saying her name. Dani.
She asked if there'd been a kid in the bar that night.

It took him a while. A kid. On a Series night. Then, slower: I told you. I couldn't see over the people. That guy was yelling down at something, by the hallway. Another wait. Down. The fryer again. Your dad, every time he came up, I poured a beer and a Sprite. Later on just the Sprite.

Who was the Sprite for, she asked. He'd figured one of Luis's guys was driving, he said. Then nothing, just him breathing on the line. I never once thought about who it was for, he said. Not once, Dani.
She thanked him. She didn't remember hanging up.

The prep book was in the glove box, and the envelope was still in it, marking her page. MAYBE HE DID IT across the top, in her own capitals. NEEDED. ENOUGH. HE SWUNG FIRST. Since December she'd only ever written on that one side.
She turned it over. Nothing on the back. She wrote on it.
Her phone buzzed in her lap. Teo.
A text from Teo. how is he
He hadn't asked about their father in ten years.
She typed one word and looked at it a while. Then two more lines, because the last one was true and it was Teo's more than hers, and she sent it before she could fix anything.
A text from Dani. tired. he asked about you. he said you always took with the wrong pawn
Three dots came up. They went away. They came back for a second, and went away again, and stayed gone.

She laid the envelope on the dash with the new side down, so the old side looked up at her, MAYBE HE DID IT in her own capitals, and backed out. Past the fences, out to 61, then 76, two hours with the sun in her eyes most of the way. It rode like that the whole way home. She knew what was on the other side.
